page3_img_1.png.title: Project coverage in Developers vs. Lines-of-Code space
page3_img_1.png.description: A two-panel schematic that maps a universe of projects (points) by #developers (x axis) and #lines of code (y axis). In (a) project A is enlarged and shown with light-gray horizontal and vertical bands (dashed borders) that mark projects similar to A on each single dimension; the darker square at their intersection marks projects similar to A in both dimensions (A plus seven others → 8/50 = 16% universe coverage; per-dimension coverage: developers 13/50 = 26%, lines-of-code 11/50 = 22%). Panel (b) contrasts two possible additions: project B (lower-left) has a neighborhood that covers many previously uncovered projects and so raises total coverage to 18/50 = 36% (with developer and LOC dimension coverage rising to 60% and 56%), whereas project C (near A, arrowed) overlaps A’s neighborhood and adds little new coverage.

page5_img_2.png.title: Cumulative coverage vs. number of projects (Ohloh universe)
page5_img_2.png.description: A log‑scale cumulative plot showing how coverage of the 20,028‑project Ohloh universe grows as projects are greedily added by the next_projects algorithm. The x‑axis is the number of projects (log scale) and the y‑axis is the coverage score (fraction of the universe covered); individual points are the cumulative coverage after adding each next project. Two annotations highlight that the first 50 projects cover 15.3% of the universe and that 392 projects cover 50.0%, indicated by dashed vertical and horizontal guide lines. The curve rises slowly at first and then accelerates, illustrating that a small set of projects yields nontrivial coverage but many hundreds (and ultimately thousands — the paper reports 5,030 projects to reach full coverage) are required to cover the entire universe.

page5_img_1.png.title: Histograms of Ohloh project dimensions (languages, size, activity)
page5_img_1.png.description: Multi-panel horizontal bar charts showing distributions across the Ohloh universe (20,028 active projects) for main language, contributors (last 12 months), commits (last 12 months), lines of code, churn (last 12 months), project age, and activity. The language chart lists top counts: Java 3,019; Python 2,589; C 2,478; JavaScript 2,192; C++ 1,967; Ruby 1,941; PHP 1,753, with 2,288 projects grouped as “64 other languages.” The size and activity panels are heavily skewed toward small projects: 4,937 projects have 0–2K LOC, 7,235 projects had 2 contributors in the last year, and 10,528 projects had 1–50 commits in the last 12 months, while a long tail exists (e.g., 713 projects >1,000K LOC, 13 projects with >500 contributors, and 47 projects with churn >10M). Project age and activity bins show most projects are “Normal” age (9,021); activity is split with 8,046 showing no change, 6,583 decreasing, and 5,399 increasing.

page6_img_1.png.title: Coverage and per-dimension representativeness for ICSE/FSE papers and five exemplar studies
page6_img_1.png.description: A table with horizontal orange bars and numeric labels that reports the overall coverage score and seven per-dimension coverage percentages for two sets: “All papers of ICSE and FSE (past 2 years)” and five individual papers (Gabel & Su; Apel et al.; Beck & Diehl; Uddin et al.; Jin & Orso). The leftmost column shows that the combined ICSE/FSE papers cover 9.15% of the Ohloh universe overall, while per-dimension coverage for that column is very high: Main language 91.42%, Total lines of code 99.29%, Contributors 100.00%, Churn 98.08%, Commits 100.00%, Project age 100.00%, and Project activity 100.00%. The five exemplar papers have much smaller overall scores (1.09% down to 0.67%) but often high coverage on operational dimensions (e.g., contributors ~97–99.9%, commits ~56–97.98%, activity frequently 100%); by contrast, programming-language and total‑lines coverage vary widely across papers (e.g., Beck & Diehl main language 15.07%, Gabel & Su total lines 65.82%, Jin & Orso project activity 59.83%). The visualization highlights the contrast between low overall (all-dimensions) representativeness and generally strong coverage on several individual dimensions.
